“‘Ah, very well; that settles the matter completely. What a pity, for in other respects you really would have suited us very well. In that case, Miss Stoper, I had better see a few more of your young ladies.’

“Throughout this exchange the manageress had sat busy with her papers, without speaking to either of us. Now she glanced at me with such an annoyed expression that I could not help suspecting my refusal had cost her a handsome commission.
“‘Do you want us to keep your name on our books?’ she asked.
“‘Yes, please, Miss Stoper.’

“‘Really, that seems pointless if you reject excellent offers in this fashion,’ she snapped. ‘You can hardly expect us to work hard to find you another opportunity like this. Good day, Miss Hunter.’ She struck the gong on her desk, and the page showed me out.

“Back at my lodgings, Mr. Holmes, I found a nearly empty cupboard and two or three bills on the table. I began to wonder whether I had been foolish. These people might have odd whims and demand obedience in extraordinary matters, but they were willing to pay for their eccentricities. Few governesses in England earn a hundred pounds a year. And what good was my hair to me? Short hair improves many people; perhaps it would improve me. The next day I suspected I had made a mistake. By the day after, I was certain. I had almost swallowed my pride enough to return to the agency and ask whether the post remained available when the gentleman himself wrote. I have his letter here with me, and I shall read it to you:
“‘The Copper Beeches, near Winchester.

“‘Dear Miss Hunter,—Miss Stoper kindly supplied your address. Have you reconsidered your decision? My wife is most eager for you to come, having been greatly impressed by my description. We will pay thirty pounds a quarter, or a hundred and twenty a year, to compensate for any inconvenience our little fancies cause. They are not very demanding. My wife likes a particular electric-blue shade and would like you to wear a dress of that colour indoors during the morning. There is no need to buy one: we have a dress belonging to my dear daughter Alice, now in Philadelphia, which I believe would fit you perfectly. Sitting in particular places or amusing yourself as we suggest should cause no difficulty. As for your hair, cutting it is certainly a pity. Even in our brief meeting I noticed its beauty. Nevertheless, I must insist on this point and hope the higher salary will compensate for your loss. Your duties towards the child will be light. Please try to come. I shall meet you at Winchester with the dog-cart. Tell me which train you will take. Yours faithfully,
“‘JEPHRO RUCASTLE.’

“That is the letter I have just received, Mr. Holmes, and I have decided to accept the offer. Before taking the final step, however, I thought I should like to lay the whole matter before you for consideration.”
“If your decision is made, Miss Hunter, that settles the question,” Holmes replied, smiling.
“You would not advise me to refuse?”
“I admit it is not a position I would want a sister of mine to seek.”
“What can it all mean, Mr. Holmes?”
“I have no evidence to guide me. Perhaps you have formed an opinion yourself?”

“Well, it seems to me that only one explanation is possible. Mr. Rucastle appeared a very kind and good-natured man. Could his wife be mad, and could he want to conceal the fact for fear she would be sent to an asylum, indulging her every fancy to prevent an outburst?”
“That is a possible explanation—indeed, with the information we have, the most likely one. In any event, though, it hardly sounds a pleasant household for a young woman.”
“But the money, Mr. Holmes! The money!”

“Well, yes, the salary is certainly generous—too generous. That is what troubles me. Why pay you a hundred and twenty pounds a year when forty would give them their choice? There must be a powerful reason behind it.”
“I thought that if I explained everything now, you would understand later if I needed help. Knowing you were behind me would give me so much more courage.”

“You can certainly leave here with that assurance. Your little problem promises to be the most interesting that has come my way for several months. Some of its features are distinctly original. If you find yourself uncertain or in danger—”
“Danger! What sort of danger do you expect?”
Holmes shook his head seriously. “If we could define it, it would cease to be dangerous. But whenever you need me, day or night, a telegram will bring me to your assistance.”

“That is all I need.” She rose promptly, anxiety gone from her face. “I can go to Hampshire with an easy mind now. I shall write to Mr. Rucastle immediately, sacrifice my poor hair tonight, and leave for Winchester tomorrow.” After thanking Holmes, she wished us both good night and hurried away.
“At least,” I said, as we heard her quick, firm footsteps going down the stairs, “she seems a young woman quite capable of taking care of herself.”
“She will need to be,” Holmes replied gravely. “Unless I am badly mistaken, we shall hear from her again within a few days.”

It was not very long before my friend’s prediction proved correct. Two weeks passed, and I often found my thoughts turning towards her, wondering what strange corner of human experience this solitary woman had entered. The exceptional salary, peculiar demands, and light workload all suggested something abnormal. Whether it was a whim or a scheme, whether the employer was a benefactor or a villain, I could not decide. Holmes often sat for half an hour at a stretch looking distant and frowning. But whenever I mentioned the matter, he waved it aside. ‘Facts! Facts! Facts!’ he exclaimed impatiently. ‘I cannot make bricks without clay.’ Yet he always ended by muttering that no sister of his should ever have taken such a post.

The telegram finally arrived late one night, just as I was thinking of going to bed and Holmes was settling down to one of his frequent all-night chemical investigations. On such nights I would leave him bent over a retort and a test tube, and find him in the same position when I came down for breakfast. He opened the yellow envelope, glanced at the message and tossed it across to me.
“Look up the trains in Bradshaw,” he said, returning to his chemical work.
The message was short and urgent.
“Please meet me at the Black Swan Hotel, Winchester, at noon tomorrow. Do come! I do not know what to do.
“HUNTER.”
“Will you accompany me?” Holmes asked, looking up.
“I would like to.”
“Then find the train.”
“One leaves at half-past nine,” I said, consulting Bradshaw. “It reaches Winchester at half-past eleven.”
“That will suit us perfectly. Perhaps I should put off my acetone analysis. We may need all our powers tomorrow morning.”

By eleven o’clock the following day we were well on our way to England’s old capital. Holmes had remained absorbed in the morning newspapers throughout the journey, but once we crossed the Hampshire border he threw them down and began admiring the scenery. It was a perfect spring day, with a light blue sky dotted by small, fleecy white clouds drifting from west to east. The sun shone brilliantly, yet an invigorating chill in the air gave a keen edge to one’s energy. All across the countryside, towards the rolling hills around Aldershot, small red and grey farm roofs peeped through the light green of the new leaves.
“How fresh and beautiful they look!” I exclaimed with the enthusiasm of a man newly escaped from Baker Street’s fog.
Holmes, however, shook his head solemnly.

“Do you know, Watson,” he said, “one curse of a mind of my particular kind is that I must view everything in relation to my own special subject? You look at those scattered houses and are struck by their beauty. I look at them and can think only of their isolation, and how crimes might be committed there without fear of punishment.”
“Good heavens!” I cried. “Who would connect these charming old farmhouses with crime?”

“They always fill me with a certain dread. I believe, on the strength of my experience, Watson, that the lowest and vilest alleys of London have no more dreadful record of wickedness than this beautiful, smiling countryside.”
“That is a horrible thought!”

“But the reason is perfectly plain. In a town, the pressure of public opinion can achieve what the law cannot. Even in the vilest alley, the scream of a tortured child or the thud of a drunkard’s blow arouses sympathy and outrage among the neighbours. And the whole machinery of justice is so close that a single complaint can set it in motion: there is only a step from the crime to the dock. Now look at these lonely houses, each standing in its own fields, mostly occupied by poor, ignorant people who know little about the law. Think of the acts of hellish cruelty, the hidden wickedness, that could continue year after year in such places, with no one any the wiser. Had the lady seeking our help gone to live in Winchester, I should never have feared for her. Those five miles of countryside create the danger. Still, it is clear that she is not personally threatened.”
“No. If she can meet us in Winchester, she can leave the house.”
“Exactly. She remains free to go.”
“Then what _can_ be wrong? Can you offer no explanation?”

“I have devised seven separate explanations, each of which fits the facts as far as we know them. But only the fresh information that doubtless awaits us can establish which is correct. Well, there is the cathedral tower, and we shall soon hear everything Miss Hunter has to tell us.”
The Black Swan is a well-regarded inn in the High Street, not far from the station. There we found the young woman waiting for us. She had hired a sitting-room, and our lunch was ready on the table.
“I am so glad you came,” she said earnestly. “It is very kind of you both. Truly, I do not know what to do. Your advice will be invaluable.”
“Please tell us what has been happening.”
“I will, and quickly: I promised to return before three. Mr. Rucastle allowed me to come into town this morning, though he had no idea why I wanted to.”
“Let us hear everything in its proper order.” Holmes stretched his long, thin legs towards the fire and settled down to listen.

“First of all, I should say that, on the whole, I have suffered no actual ill-treatment from Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle. It is only fair to acknowledge that. But I cannot understand them, and I feel uneasy about them.”
